sections.title: Reinforcement and punishment explained: positive and negative

blocks.x: Reinforcement and punishment are terms from behaviour psychology. They describe what happens after a behaviour and how that changes the chance that it happens again. They are easy to confuse, so this article explains them with classroom examples.

items: Did something get added (positive) or removed (negative)?

blocks.x: Positive does not mean good, and negative does not mean bad. Negative reinforcement is not a kind of punishment.

When a behaviour no longer gets the reward that kept it going, it usually becomes less frequent. For example, if a learner calls out and you do not respond, but you do respond when the learner raises a hand, calling out may decrease. The behaviour sometimes gets worse for a short time before it improves.

Positive discipline is an approach to guiding behaviour that aims to teach learners self-discipline and life skills, with respect for both the teacher and the learner. It is not the same as positive punishment, which is a technical term from behaviour psychology.

The approach builds on the work of the psychologists Alfred Adler and Rudolf Dreikurs. Jane Nelsen and others developed it into the Positive Discipline programme for families and classrooms. Cambodia's Ministry of Education has produced child-friendly school materials and has run teacher training on positive discipline.
Jane Nelsen describes five criteria for discipline that teaches. Effective discipline:

items: Helps learners feel connected, with a sense of belonging and significance.
Is kind and firm at the same time, respectful and encouraging.
Is effective in the long term. Punishment may work in the short term, but its long-term results can be negative.
Teaches valuable social and life skills, such as respect, problem-solving, cooperation and responsibility.
Helps learners discover that they are capable.
Firm: you keep the limit and follow through calmly.
Kind: you respect the learner, listen and avoid shame.
Example: I can see you want to talk to your friend. We can talk after the task. For now, please work on your own.
Connection before correction: a friendly word first.
Offer choices within limits.
Ask what and how questions: What happened? What could you do next time?
Look for solutions together.
Treat mistakes as chances to learn.
Use encouragement that notices effort and improvement.
Hold class meetings to solve problems together.
